notes:
I've written verse-by-verse notes on Obadiah 1 below, but coverage is uneven. My tool budget ran out before I could read several of the sources you listed, so I found nothing from Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan or Orthodox teachers, nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching, and only the opening of the Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Some verses (6, 9, 13, 19, 20) have little or no comment of their own. Where a page I read in full gave no sentence references, I've summarised it and given the URL.

**Background (whole book)**
- Edom came from Esau, Jacob's twin. The enmity between the brothers ran on through their descendants. Judah, not Edom, is the main audience: God is assuring Judah he hasn't forgotten the wrongs done to them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/obadiah-commentary
- **The date is debated, and this is the main divide in the book:**
  - **Early date:** Guzik (Calvary Chapel; enduringword.com is on your Pentecostal/charismatic list) prefers the attack under King Jehoram, because verses 10–14 doesn't seem to indicate that Jerusalem was totally destroyed, as it was under the Babylonian attack. That makes Obadiah the earliest of the writing prophets. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/obadiah/obadiah-1.cfm. GotQuestions also dates it between 848 and 840 BC, following an invasion of the Philistines and Arabians. https://www.gotquestions.org/Book-of-Obadiah.html
  - **Exile date:** Ligonier (Reformed) dates it at the time of the exile of Judah into Babylon. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/word-lord-edom
  - **NET Bible note** (quoted on Precept Austin): most modern scholars reject a ninth-century date. The Babylonian setting is held by "many biblical scholars from Luther to the present"; it fits but can't be proven. The note says the closeness to Jeremiah 49 might point to the sixth century. https://www.preceptaustin.org/obadiah-commentary
  - **Bible Odyssey (modern scholarship):** Edom is punished for participating in the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BCE. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/obadiah-the-book-of/
  - **Ellicott:** verse 11 is too general to tie to one capture of Jerusalem, but he leans toward the early years of the exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/obadiah/1.htm
- **TGC (Busenitz):** the theme is the Day of the LORD. Verses 15–21 look beyond historical Edom to any nation that opposes God's purposes. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/obadiah/
- **Catholic Encyclopedia:** "Abdias" is the Greek form of the Hebrew name, meaning "the servant [or worshipper] of Yahweh". https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/Abdias-(Obadiah)
- **Ellicott:** compared with other prophecies against Edom (Isaiah 34, Psalm 137), Obadiah is unusually free of revenge. He hears a note of regret, perhaps a sense of brotherhood with Esau. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/obadiah/1.htm

**v. 1**
- "Vision" means a message from God, not the prophet's own thoughts. "Lord GOD" (Adonai Yahweh) stresses God's rule over all creation. God himself calls the nations to carry out his judgment on Edom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/obadiah-commentary
- Guzik calls it a "news bulletin" from the LORD. He thinks Jeremiah probably had Obadiah in front of him, because verses 1–9 closely match Jeremiah 49:7–22. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/obadiah/obadiah-1.cfm
- Ellicott counts four verses of Jeremiah 49 that are identical to verses in Obadiah. He says that if the relationship between the two could be settled, the book's date would be settled too. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/obadiah/1.htm

**v. 2**
- Because of the coming battle, God will make Edom small among the nations and greatly despised. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/obadiah-1/
- Ellicott notes that the KJV reads "I have made you small" (past tense). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/obadiah/1.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik says Edom was a small, relatively poor and insignificant nation, yet it boasted in its natural defences. He points to Petra (Sela), a city carved into rock and reached through a canyon almost a mile long. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/obadiah/obadiah-1.cfm
- Busenitz describes Edom's rugged land as an "impenetrable defense," backed by copper mining and tolls from the King's Highway. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/obadiah/
- Spurgeon (Baptist) preached on this verse as "Self-deceived": pride is self-deceit. He adds that those who are sure that they have no pride are probably the proudest of all. https://www.preceptaustin.org/obadiah-devotionals-and-sermon-illustrations

**v. 4**
- Busenitz: verse 4 answers the proud boast of verse 3. The picture is of birds nesting in the inaccessible crevices of the sheer mountain walls surrounding Edom. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/obadiah/
- Guzik's application: God can bring us down anytime. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/obadiah/obadiah-1.cfm
- Ellicott calls this image one of "almost startling boldness." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/obadiah/1.htm

**vv. 5–6**
- Guzik: thieves usually stop once they have enough, but Edom's judgment will be far worse than an ordinary robbery. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Oba/Oba-1.cfm
- Ellicott hears regret in the cry "oh, how you will be ruined!" in verse 5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/obadiah/1.htm

**v. 7**
- Precept Austin: those at peace with Edom would betray her. The Hebrew verb means to trick, which stresses the use of treachery rather than force alone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/obadiah-commentary
- Guzik: Edom trusted its alliances, but it would be double-crossed by their former friends. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/obadiah-1/

**vv. 8–9**
- Edom was famous for wisdom, especially the city of Teman. Guzik cites 1 Kings 4:30 on the "men of the East" and Jeremiah 49:7. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/obadiah-1/
- Busenitz: Job's friend Eliphaz came from Teman. The lack of understanding in verse 7 is explained by God destroying Edom's wise men in verse 8. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/obadiah/

**v. 10**
- Guzik: Edom and Israel share an ancestor in Isaac, which made Edom's sin against Israel all the worse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/obadiah-1/
- Busenitz: calling Israel "Jacob" takes the reader back to the birth of the twins (Genesis 25). He adds that Israel had been told to be kind to Edom (Deuteronomy 23:7). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/obadiah/
- Guzik sees "cut off forever" fulfilled: Edomites joined the Jewish revolt of AD 66–70 and were crushed by Rome, never to be heard of as a people again. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/obadiah/obadiah-1.cfm
- GotQuestions instead places the fulfilment in the fifth century B.C. when Edom was removed from Petra. https://www.gotquestions.org/Edom-Obadiah.html

**v. 11**
- Precept Austin: Edom's sin wasn't just watching. Edom identified herself with the victors rather than with her covenant brother. https://www.preceptaustin.org/obadiah-commentary
- Guzik: Sometimes doing nothing is a great sin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/obadiah/obadiah-1.cfm

**vv. 12–14 (the steps of Edom's sin)**
- Busenitz: the prophet uses eight "do not" commands. First Edom ignored Judah's need (v. 11), then gloated (v. 12), then looted (v. 13), then blocked Judah's escape (v. 14). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/obadiah/
- Guzik traces the same slide: doing nothing, then pride, then plunder, then violence. He quotes Trapp: "Sin proceeds by degrees; neither is any man at his worst at first." In verse 14, Edomites met refugees fleeing south and either killed them or handed them to the enemy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/obadiah/obadiah-1.cfm
- v. 13, Precept Austin: repeating "the day of their disaster" stresses that this was exactly when Edom should have shown compassion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/obadiah-commentary
- **Grammar point (Ellicott):** in verses 13–14 the Hebrew is really "do not look," not "you should not have" (the Authorised Version). He takes this to mean the prophet is listing Edom's habitual tactics. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/obadiah/1.htm

**v. 15**
- Guzik: God gives Edom simple justice. So if we want mercy from God, we do well to give mercy to others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/obadiah-1/
- **Distinctive application (Guzik):** he links the verse to Genesis 12:3 and concludes, "If we want to be blessed, we should bless the Jewish people." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Oba/Oba-1.cfm
- **Dispensational reading:** a Precept Austin page argues that the Day of the Lord in Obadiah and Isaiah 34 must be future. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_peter_310. Busenitz, also quoted there, sees Edom's historical judgment as a preview of his future judgment on all nations who refuse to bow to the LORD. https://www.preceptaustin.org/obadiah-commentary

**v. 16 (who is drinking?)**
- **Busenitz:** "you" is singular in verse 15 but plural in verse 16, so the prophet seems to be making a brief reference to Judah. The nations will cease as nations, but a believing remnant of the nations, including Edom, will survive (Jeremiah 49:11). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/obadiah/
- **Ellicott** agrees: the natural reading is the cup of suffering, which must have been drained by Israelites, as Ewald and others take the passage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/obadiah/1.htm
- **Another view (Precept Austin):** the verse describes Edom's drinking parties turning into the cup of God's wrath. Within a few years Edom was destroyed by Gentile powers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/obadiah-commentary
- **Spurgeon:** the verse shows contempt for holy things. God will not have his church made into a tavern, or a playhouse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/obadiah-devotionals-and-sermon-illustrations

**v. 17**
- Guzik: the troubles of God's people are only temporary, because among them there shall be deliverance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/obadiah-1/
- Ellicott: while judgment falls on the nations, Mount Zion will be a refuge for scattered Israelites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/obadiah/1.htm
- Spurgeon preached "Possessing Possessions" on this verse. While Edom kept raiding, Israel couldn't enjoy its own harvests in peace; with Edom's rule ended, that barrier would be gone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/obadiah-devotionals-and-sermon-illustrations

**v. 18**
- Busenitz: earlier God used the nations against Edom (vv. 1, 7). Now the escaped remnant will be divinely empowered to dispose of the house of Esau. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/obadiah/
- Guzik sees this "precisely fulfilled," noting You just won't meet an Edomite today. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/obadiah/obadiah-1.cfm

**vv. 19–20 (the land)**
- **Futurist reading (Guzik):** Israel will one day hold Esau's land. Though modern Israel's borders don't include Edom, we can trust that they one day will, either in this age or in the age to come. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/obadiah-1/
- **Ellicott:** "house of Jacob" here means Judah. He reads the restored kingdom of Zion as covering the land then held by the Idumeans. He infers from verse 20 that the prophet was probably among the captives himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/obadiah/1-21.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/obadiah/1.htm
- **Older Jewish reading (reported by Ellicott):** the rabbis held that Edom means Rome and all Christians. They read verses 20–21 as foretelling Christianity's downfall and Jewish conquest of France and Spain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/obadiah/1.htm

**v. 21 (the clearest split between interpreters)**
- **Guzik:** "saviors" has the sense of "deliverers." Edom has no deliverer, but Zion does. They judge Edom in three ways: by Edom having no deliverers, by ruling its land, and by sitting in judgment on its sins. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/obadiah-1/
- **Barnes, Pulpit, Ellicott, Poole and Clarke:** the immediate meaning is historical leaders, such as Zerubbabel, Ezra, Nehemiah and the Maccabees. Barnes and the Pulpit add that these were types pointing to Christ. Poole reads them "mystically" as Christ and his apostles, and other preachers of the gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/obadiah/1-21.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/obadiah/1-21.html
- **Gill (Baptist):** it is "best" to read the saviours as apostles and gospel preachers, especially in the last days. He reads Edom as the antichrist. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/obadiah/1-21.htm
- **Matthew Henry (on StudyLight):** ministers are saviours when they preach that whoever believes will be saved, and they "judge Esau" when they warn that unbelievers will be condemned. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/obadiah/1-21.html
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** in the kingdom to come there will be no king, but a prince; the sabbatic period of the judges will return. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/obadiah/1-21.html
- **Baker (Tyndale, as summarised by Rosscup):** sees verse 21 fulfilled by a king on earth after the Second Advent. https://www.preceptaustin.org/Micah_commentaries
- **A devotional on Precept Austin:** links the "deliverers" to Christ's promises that his apostles will help him rule (Matthew 19:28). https://www.preceptaustin.org/obadiah-devotionals-and-sermon-illustrations
- **Translation of "saviours" (Pulpit):** the Greek Old Testament wrongly took the word as passive, "those who are saved." Symmachus and the Latin Vulgate (*salvatores*) rightly have "saviours." https://biblehub.com/obadiah/1-21.htm
- **Ellicott:** as the vision widens, Zion and Edom both drop from view. Both are taken into one divine kingdom, and God is all in all. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/obadiah/1-21.html
- **G. Campbell Morgan (on Precept Austin):** at the end the prophet sees God's sovereignty bringing deliverance even to Edom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/obadiah-devotionals-and-sermon-illustrations
